locator.heading: Wild Thyme, Or Mother Of Thyme

source_text:
WILD Thyme also is so well known, that it needs no description.

_Place._] It may be found commonly in commons, and other barren places
throughout the nation.

_Government and virtues._] It is under the dominion of Venus, and
under the sign Aries, and therefore chiefly appropriated to the head.
It provokes urine and the terms, and eases the griping pain of the
belly, cramps, ruptures, and inflamation of the liver. If you make a
vinegar of the herb, as vinegar of roses is made (you may find out
the way in my translation of the London Dispensatory) and anoint the
head with it, it presently stops the pains thereof. It is excellently
good to be given either in phrenzy or lethargy, although they are two
contrary diseases: It helps spitting and voiding of blood, coughing,
and vomiting; it comforts and strengthens the head, stomach, reins, and
womb, expels wind, and breaks the stone.

evidence.summary: Modern evidence supports Thymus serpyllum's traditional use for respiratory issues like coughing and digestive complaints such as belly pain, primarily due to thymol and carvacrol. While specific historical claims regarding liver inflammation or head pains lack direct modern clinical validation, the plant's broad antimicrobial and anti-inflammatory properties provide a plausible mechanistic basis for these ancient observations.

concordance.rationale: Modern evidence (PMID: 38174535) confirms traditional use but lacks clinical data for specific claims like headache or stone-breaking. Pharmacological plausibility exists for antimicrobial effects, not analgesia.
concordance.uncertainty: High uncertainty due to absence of randomized controlled trials for the specific historical indications listed in the entry.
caveats: No clinical proof for headache relief.
